title: Is Perfectionism a Problem?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. offers a practitioner's-lens analysis of perfectionism, beginning with the APA definition and unpacking three key terms — tendency, demand, and 'in excess of what is required by the situation.' He identifies six ways perfectionism harms teachers: creating pressure, setting unrealistic standards, draining time and energy, increasing risk-aversion, harming relationships, and blocking growth through failure. The article closes with four practical counter-strategies drawn from Stuart's own experience managing perfectionist tendencies, including acknowledging it, sharing it with a trusted person, using Jedi mind tricks from an earlier article, and chuckling at the self-contradiction of trying to perfectly eliminate perfectionism.
points: Perfectionism operates as a soul-level demand — not a high standard but an unforgiving taskmaster that punishes deviation and is clinically linked to depression, anxiety, and eating disorders.
The APA phrase 'in excess of what is required by the situation' is the operative criterion: high expectations become perfectionism only when they exceed what the context actually demands.

Perfectionism blocks risk-taking because risking failure threatens a teacher's core professional identity, creating a perverse incentive to avoid the growth opportunities that come through difficulty.
A first-year mentor's advice — 'You're not supposed to do it all; you have to decide' — is the practical antidote that satisficing later formalizes into a professional discipline.

The student-teacher failure story at University of Michigan becomes the article's fulcrum: failure is the medium for growth when perfectionism does not block the learner's perception of what went wrong.
quotes: perfectionism. n. the tendency to demand of others or of oneself an extremely high or even flawless level of performance, in excess of what is required by the situation. It is associated with depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and other mental health problems.
Demand — Here's the core problem engine of perfectionism. It acts like a soul-level demand and can become a draconian taskmaster. It is not merciful or gracious.
They create large amounts of pressure, on both the perfectionist and the object of their perfectionism. I need lots of things in a given day of teaching, but more pressure isn't one of them.

I remember being the most unsuccessful student teacher in my cohort at the University of Michigan. I had intentionally sought a difficult student teaching placement, and I sure got one! The problem is, I wasn't up to the challenge.

At least I learned some things that DON'T work today. And that sentiment really struck me; it's got to be the most profound realization I had in all of college. The perfectionistic side of me can't handle failure; but when I set him aside and give him a Miller Lite to soothe himself, the other part can turn even the worst failure into a means of growth.
